title: Why did the industry move beyond synchronous REST for long-running workflows (thread blocking, thread-pool exhaustion, HTTP 202 Accepted, accept-then-process), and what does async communication actually improve?
shortTitle: Why did the industry move beyond synchronous REST for long-running workflows
keyPoints: Synchronous REST holds a thread for the entire job duration, and the thread is mostly idle waiting on I/O
Thread-pool exhaustion occurs when all threads are blocked, making the service appear down at low CPU
The accept-then-process pattern returns HTTP 202 Accepted with a tracking handle immediately
The queue acts as a shock absorber: producers burst while consumers drain at a steady rate
Async improves throughput, decoupling, failure isolation, and user experience for long work
Idempotency keys prevent duplicate work when the client retries the accept call
Status tracking and notification replace the inline response for genuinely long workflows

s1_definition.oneliner: Synchronous REST ties up a thread for the entire job and exhausts the pool under load, so for long work we accept-then-process, return 202 with a handle, and finish asynchronously.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Thread blocking** – synchronous REST holds a thread from request arrival until response, even though the thread is mostly idle waiting on I/O.
- **Thread-pool exhaustion** – when all threads are blocked on slow work, new requests queue and time out even at low CPU.
- **Accept-then-process** – validate, persist a PENDING record, enqueue the job, and return HTTP 202 Accepted immediately.
- **Tracking handle** – the 202 response includes a status URL or job ID the client can poll or subscribe to.
- **Shock absorber** – the queue absorbs bursts while consumers drain at a steady rate.
- **Idempotency** – the client attaches a key so retrying the accept call does not create duplicate work.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine Rajesh asks the bank teller to process a complex international transfer that takes ten minutes of back-office checks. In the synchronous model the teller stands frozen at the counter for ten minutes, and the queue behind Rajesh grows until the whole branch jams. In the asynchronous model the teller takes the form, hands Rajesh a token number, says "we will notify you", and immediately serves the next customer while the back office does the slow work. The counter never freezes.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Synchronous REST (WRONG for long work):
  Client ──POST──> Thread blocked 30-90s ──> Response
                   (pool exhausted)

  Accept-then-Process (CORRECT):
  Client ──POST──> Validate + Persist + Enqueue ──> 202 Accepted
                   (10ms, thread freed)              + status URL
                              │
                              ▼
                   ┌─────────────────────┐
                   │    Kafka Queue      │
                   │  (shock absorber)   │
                   └──────────┬──────────┘
                              │
                   ┌──────────▼──────────┐
                   │  Background Workers  │
                   │  SWIFT, fraud, etc.  │
                   │  (scale independently)│
                   └──────────┬──────────┘
                              │
                              ▼
                   Update status: COMPLETED
                   Notify client (webhook or poll)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The industry moved beyond synchronous REST for long-running workflows because of thread-pool exhaustion. A server has a bounded pool of worker threads, and synchronous REST holds one thread per request until the response is written. For a workflow taking seconds or minutes, the thread is mostly idle waiting on I/O, so you can exhaust all threads while the CPU sits nearly idle, and simple balance checks start failing even though the machine is not overloaded.

The fix is the accept-then-process pattern: validate the input, persist a durable PENDING record with an idempotency key, enqueue the job, and return HTTP 202 Accepted with a status URL. The request thread is freed in milliseconds. The queue acts as a shock absorber, absorbing bursts while background workers drain at a steady rate. The client either polls the status endpoint or receives a webhook when the work completes.

At National Bank of India, international transfers involving SWIFT and correspondent banks took 30 to 90 seconds. The synchronous endpoint held threads for the whole duration, and during a morning spike the pool filled while simple balance checks started failing. We rebuilt it as accept-then-process with an idempotency key, and the API stayed fast, duplicates disappeared, and operations could retry failed jobs from the durable record.

Remember one sentence: synchronous REST exhausts the thread pool under long-running load even at low CPU, so for long work return 202 with a tracking handle and complete asynchronously, which gives throughput, decoupling, and a responsive API.
